records.question: Did the DOE reactor pilot program get three test reactors to criticality by July 4, 2026?
records.answer: Yes, by DOE's own count. DOE selected 11 projects on August 12, 2025 with a goal of at least three test reactors reaching criticality by July 4, 2026. DOE reported Deployable Energy's Unity as the pilot's third criticality (June 30, 2026, announced July 1, 2026). DOE reported Aalo Atomics' Aalo-X as the pilot's fourth criticality (July 4, 2026, announced July 6, 2026). DOE later called Oklo's Groves (early August) the fifth that summer. The library does not name the first two, and the count is DOE's, not an independent census; criticality is a test milestone, not a commercial license or power delivery.

records.question: Which Reserve Bank runs which national payment and Treasury service?
records.answer: The Fed's national services are spread across the twelve Reserve Banks, each a separate legal corporation. Boston runs FedNow; New York runs Fedwire Funds, Fedwire Securities and the National Settlement Service and carries out the Fed's open-market operations; Atlanta runs check and FedACH; Chicago runs FedLine access; Cleveland builds Treasury's Pay.gov; Minneapolis supports TreasuryDirect; Richmond hosts the System's national IT; Kansas City decides account requests.

records.question: When can an investment adviser hold clients' crypto keys itself under the SEC proposal?
records.answer: Only as a last resort, and only if the proposal becomes final; the SEC proposed it on October 1, 2026 and no final rule has been issued. For an ordinary advisory client the rule reaches a crypto asset only when it is a fund or security. The adviser may hold the keys itself only when, after a written inquiry, no qualified custodian will hold that particular asset (cost does not count), re-checked at least quarterly, and it must move the asset to a custodian as soon as reasonably practicable once one is available. Only designated supervised people may hold key material, every movement needs at least two of them including a management person, and a technology vendor must not be able to reach the keys or move the assets alone, so a single-employee adviser cannot use the route.

records.question: Which crypto technologies could fit the SEC's tokenized-stock exemption, and has anyone actually started?
records.answer: Plenty could fit, but no one has started under the order. The library reads 20 core systems and 14 added ones against the ten seats an exempt venue needs: 4 are core technical candidates (Ethereum, Stellar, Solana, Algorand), 8 conditional candidates, 5 supporting layers and 3 outside the core design. The only public step so far is Imperium's filing as a prospective liquidity provider on September 28, 2026; it says it has not begun, and no venue notice or launch was found through October 5, 2026.

records.question: What does the SEC's tokenized-stock exemption allow, and how big can it get?
records.answer: SEC Release No. 34-106402, in effect September 17, 2026 through September 17, 2031, lets a qualifying U.S. tokenized securities venue trade tokenized versions of listed U.S. stocks in permissioned automated-market-maker pools on a public, permissionless blockchain without being an 'exchange', and lets firms supplying those pools with their own capital avoid 'dealer' status. Every pair must include a tokenized stock. Size is capped at 75 symbols and 0.25% of prior-month average daily volume for S&P 500, Russell 1000 and qualifying LULD ETPs (Tier 1), and 250 symbols and 2.5% for other eligible NMS stocks (Tier 2). It approves no venue, token or chain; custody, transfer-agent, clearing and settlement law still apply.

records.question: What does Securitize actually run, and which of its companies holds which license?
records.answer: Securitize runs the official ownership record for tokenized funds and stocks, not the money. Through 6 separate companies it acts as an SEC-registered transfer agent, a broker-dealer with a trading system, an investment adviser, a fund administrator and an EU trading-and-settlement operator; each license belongs to that one subsidiary, not to the listed parent.

records.question: Who can freeze, burn or block a stablecoin?
records.answer: For 18 of the 36 crypto dollars here, the issuer can freeze or block coins, usually for suspected crime or on a court or government order. The GENIUS Act requires payment-stablecoin issuers to be able to do this.

records.question: Where does stablecoin interest go if the law bans paying it?
records.answer: The GENIUS Act bars an issuer from paying holders interest just for holding the coin. 10 of the 17 issuers here say in their terms that holders get nothing, and 7 don't say. The interest earned on the reserves stays with the issuer, which shares much of it with distributors such as exchanges. Some of those distributors pay their own customers 'rewards', and whether that is allowed is the open question.

records.question: Can a stablecoin's issuer change while the coin, wallet and checkout stay the same?
records.answer: Yes. Tether moved all of USD₮'s obligations to a new company effective January 27, 2025 without users changing wallets, and SoFi's current SOFID terms already allow a substitute issuer. PayPal moved its wallet customers to PayPal Digital on May 19, 2026, but Paxos stayed PYUSD's issuer. Circle's planned move to a New York issuer, Ripple's reserve bank and Fiserv's FIUSD programs are still plans. In each case the ticker, app and checkout can stay the same while the legal party behind them changes, so the proof is a signed transfer and new terms, not the app.

records.question: Who issues each dollar stablecoin, and who holds its reserves?
records.answer: The library tracks 17 dollar coins that are, or want to be, payment stablecoins. Those with a cited size total about $271.6 billion, and USD₮ (USDT) and USDC are 94% of it. Reserves are mostly short-term Treasuries, Treasury repos, money-market funds and bank cash, held by a few large custodians named on each card.
